concepts.title: Percent as a Fraction and Converting Fractions
concepts.definition: Per cent means out of every hundred, so a percentage is just a fraction whose denominator is 100; any fraction becomes a percentage by writing it with denominator 100 or multiplying the fraction by 100, as 3/4 = 75/100 = 75 percent.
concepts.key_idea: 3 out of 4 equals 75 out of 100: percentages are fractions in disguise.

solution_steps.explain: Multiplying the part-to-whole fraction by 100 reads it per hundred.

concepts.title: Percentage of a Quantity
concepts.definition: Taking a percentage of a quantity means multiplying the quantity by the fraction over 100: 25 percent of 120 g of biscuits is 25/100 x 120 = 30 g of sugar; comparing bare percentages across different wholes is meaningless until each is applied to its own amount.
concepts.key_idea: Percent first turns into a fraction, then multiplies the whole: 35 percent of a small packet can hold less sugar than 25 percent of a big one.

concepts.title: Comparing Scores and Labels with Percentages
concepts.definition: When tests have different maximum marks, or packaged foods have different total weights, direct comparison misleads; converting each score or ingredient share to a percentage puts them on the same out-of-hundred scale, so 87.5 percent in Science beats 84 percent in English.
concepts.key_idea: 42/50 and 70/80 only compare fairly as 84 percent vs 87.5 percent.
concepts.textbook_ref: hegp201.txt lines 829-900 (Example 1 marks, Example 2 KYC labels)

solution_steps.action: convert each score to a percentage
solution_steps.explain: Divide the marks by the maximum and multiply by 100.
The larger percentage marks the better performance because both now share the same hundred-base.
Science at 87.5 percent exceeds English at 84 percent, so the Science score is better.

concepts.title: Percentage Increase and Decrease
concepts.definition: Rate of change is measured against the original amount: percentage change equals the amount of change divided by the original, times 100; tomato prices rising from 30 to 42 rupees is a 40 percent increase and footfall falling from 160 to 100 is a 37.5 percent decrease.
concepts.key_idea: Always divide by the original value: 12 on 30 is 40 percent, 60 on 160 is 37.5 percent.
question_patterns: the price of tomatoes rose from 30 to 42 rupees - find the percentage increase

solution_steps.explain: Subtract the old value from the new one.

solution_steps.action: divide by the original and take percent
solution_steps.explain: The base is always the original amount.

concepts.title: Percent Of versus Increased By
concepts.definition: Saying the new value is 165 percent of the old equals saying it increased by 65 percent, because q = p + 65 percent of p = 1.65 p; a percent-of statement and an increase statement can describe the same growth in two voices.
concepts.key_idea: 165 percent of p is the same as p plus 65 percent of p.
question_patterns: does 165 percent of the 1961 population mean the same as an increase by 65 percent - explain
express an increase of 40 percent as a percent-of statement

rewrite 120 percent of the old value as an increase percentage

solution_steps.explain: q = 165/100 x p comes from the first statement.
q = p + 65/100 x p from the second statement.
Both voices give the same multiplier, so the statements agree.

concepts.title: Profit and Loss Percentage
concepts.definition: The cost price is what the seller paid, the selling price what the buyer pays; when selling beats cost the difference is profit, otherwise loss, and profit percent is always reckoned on the cost price, as 130 rupees on 300 gives about 43.3 percent profit.
concepts.key_idea: Kishanlal buys at 300, sells at 430: profit 130, taken as a percent of 300.
concepts.textbook_ref: hegp201.txt lines 940-1000 (sweater example, Example 4 percentage profit)
question_patterns: a sweater bought at 300 rupees sells for 430 - find the percentage profit

solution_steps.explain: Subtract the cost price from the selling price.

solution_steps.action: take it as a percent of cost
solution_steps.explain: Divide by the cost price and multiply by 100.

concepts.title: Discount and Selling Price
concepts.definition: The marked price is the quoted price and the discount is the reduction offered on it; the selling price is what remains after the discount, so a 480 rupee marked sweater sold at a 50 rupee discount brings 430 rupees.
concepts.key_idea: Selling price = marked price minus discount; discount percent is taken on the marked price.
concepts.textbook_ref: hegp201.txt lines 940-960 (marked price, discount, selling price journey)

solution_steps.action: take the discount amount off the marked price
solution_steps.explain: Subtract the discount from the quoted price.

solution_steps.action: read the discount percent if asked
solution_steps.explain: Discount divided by marked price times 100 gives the rate.
